idiom_name: QObject controller (Q_PROPERTY + signals) exposed to declarative QML documents
implementation_notes: Qt's own guidance is to write the user interface in QML and push references to C++ types into it rather than manipulating QML objects from C++: the QObject-derived class with properties, methods and signals is the container, and the QML documents are declarative children that read those properties and emit signals back. State and business logic live in the controller, QML holds no source of truth, so the same markup can be driven by a stub controller in tests or edited in Qt Design Studio without touching C++. The alternative (C++ owning the widgets directly) is the QWidgets variant.
pitfalls: Walking into loaded QML objects from C++ (findChild/setProperty on items) breaks the separation the controller exists to create and couples the backend to markup object names.
State exposed through a plain getter without a NOTIFY signal gives QML no change notification, so the view silently keeps stale values; expose properties with notify and emit them.
Context properties (rootContext()->setContextProperty) are the legacy injection route and are discouraged - prefer registered types or required properties set on the root object.

variants.name: Qt Widgets: QWidget container with passive child widgets
variants.idiom_name: QWidget/QLayout subclass owning state, children driven through signals and slots
variants.implementation_notes: In the widgets stack the container is a QWidget subclass (or a page inside a QMainWindow) that owns the model and wires the children with signals and slots; the child widgets are passive - they display what they are set to and emit signals, and never reach for the data themselves. Qt's model/view classes extend the same idea to large data sets by separating model, view and delegate. Prefer this variant when the application is already a widgets application; QML is the better fit for declarative, designer-authored interfaces.
pitfalls: Child widgets that keep their own copy of the model data drift out of sync; set them from the container and treat them as output devices.
Children held as bare pointers without a parent leak or dangle; parent them to the container or hold them in owning smart pointers.
Running blocking work in a slot freezes the GUI thread - the container should delegate to a worker and marshal the result back.
